extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners analyzing news/media framing (e.g., journalism students, media scholars, civic educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guide for analyzing how news articles/frame choices shape interpretation by identifying framing elements and classifying frames (Entman's elements; Iyengar's episodic vs. thematic). Useful for content analysis of news coverage and political communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entman's four framing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles typically contain at least two of four main types of frames—frames that define a specific problem, diagnose a cause of that problem, make a moral judgment regarding that problem, and/or suggest remedies to that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for which of the four elements are present and how they interlock; Entman notes these elements “hold together in a kind of cultural logic,” cemented by custom and convention. When coding or interpreting a story, mark explicit language that defines the problem, passages that attribute causal explanations, statements that assign moral evaluation, and any proposed solutions or policy responses. Presence of multiple elements together strengthens the overall frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators to identify frames (key terms, sources, spokespersons, images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames can be identified by analyzing the combination of key terms used, the types of information sources selected (or omitted), the chosen spokespersons, and the embedded images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a multi-dimensional approach: compile salient words/phrases (lexical indicators), list who is quoted or consulted (and who is left out), note the roles/title/authority of spokespersons, and analyze visual elements that reinforce a frame. Pay attention to omissions as well as inclusions—which perspectives or facts are absent can reveal framing choices. Combine these indicators to infer the dominant frame rather than relying on any single cue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic vs. Thematic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: News is conveyed either as a stand-alone, one-time event (episodic) or as part of a broader context/trend (thematic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify coverage by whether it treats the story as an isolated incident (episodic) or situates it within long-term patterns, statistics, or structural context (thematic). Use this classification when coding pieces: episodic stories focus on individual actors/events; thematic stories emphasize systemic causes, trends, and background. Note that Iyengar found these frame types influence how audiences attribute responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess how frames shape attribution of responsibility and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of frame chosen influences attribution of causal and treatment responsibility, which strongly affects policy preferences, evaluations of leaders and institutions, and political opinions—even when public factual knowledge is low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a frame, explicitly analyze who is made responsible (individuals, organizations, systems) and how that attribution is presented. Expect episodic frames to incline audiences to assign responsibility to individuals or discrete actors, while thematic frames tend to implicate broader structural or institutional causes. Consider downstream effects on policy preferences, assessments of political performance, and civic judgments; document language and evidence that link the frame to these likely opinion outcomes.
